items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server decompresses uploaded pipeline archives without adequately bounding expanded data in affected versions. items.description:
## Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines API server's `GET /apis/v1alpha1/runs/{run_id}/nodes/{node_id}/log` handler retrieves logs without authorizing the caller against the selected run. A caller who can reach the backend and knows a victim run ID and a suitable pod or node identifier can read live or archived logs using the API server's permissions.

items.title: Forge: verifyCertificateChain() removes trusted CA certificates with the same subject from the CA store
items.description:
### Summary

When a CA store created by `pki.createCaStore()` holds two or more certificates with the same subject name, `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` permanently removes those certificates from the store while trying each one as the issuer. A peer can send any certificate that names that subject as its issuer to make all later verifications against those CA certificates fail. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (`lib/x509.js`) asks the CA store for the issuer of each certificate with `caStore.getIssuer()`. When the store holds several certificates with the same subject, `caStore.getIssuer()` returns the store's own internal array of those certificates (`caStore.certs[hash]`, built by `addCertificate()`). `verifyCertificateChain()` used that array directly as its list of candidate parents and called `parents.shift()` on it while trying each candidate.

items.title: Keycloak vulnerable to cross-site scripting (xss) via case-insensitive uri validation bypass
items.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. A remote attacker with administrative privileges, specifically those with `manage-client` permission or access to client registration endpoints, could bypass client Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) validation. This is achieved by registering a malicious client with a specially crafted redirect URI using a case-insensitive `javascript:` or `data:` scheme. This Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability allows for arbitrary code execution in the Keycloak origin when a victim clicks the crafted link, such as in the logout flow or the Admin Console.

items.title: Keycloak vulnerable to information disclosure through arbitrary filesystem path probing
items.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak. A realm administrator with the "manage-realm" role can exploit this vulnerability by submitting an arbitrary filesystem path as a keystore parameter when creating a key provider component. This allows the administrator to probe arbitrary filesystem paths, determining which files exist and are readable by the Keycloak process. This information disclosure could be used to identify high-value targets for follow-on attacks.

items.title: Keycloak allows unauthorized access to resources via uma permission ticket bypass
items.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in org.keycloak.authorization. An authenticated user with a granted User-Managed Access (UMA) permission ticket for one resource can exploit this by using a specific permission request prefix to bypass per-resource access control. This allows the user to gain unauthorized access to all resources of that type within the same resource server, even if they do not have a ticket for those specific resources. This vulnerability requires the resource server to be configured in PERMISSIVE policy enforcement mode and affects typed resources with ownerManagedAccess enabled, where no explicit policy protects the resource type. The primary consequence is unauthorized information disclosure or modification of resources.

items.title: Keycloak vulnerable to authorization bypass via incorrect uri comparison
items.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak Policy Enforcer. This vulnerability allows any authenticated user to bypass all authorization policies, including role, scope, and User-Managed Access (UMA) permission checks. By including the configured access-denied page path within a request URL, either as a path segment or a query parameter, an attacker can gain unauthorized access to protected resources.

items.title: Keycloak: Attacker can re-enable and take over disabled clients via registration access token
items.description:
### Description
A flaw was found in Keycloak's client registration service. A remote attacker, possessing a previously issued Registration Access Token (RAT), could exploit this vulnerability to re-enable a client that an administrator had explicitly disabled. This bypasses security controls, allowing the attacker to reset the client's secret and potentially regain privileged API access. The primary impact includes unauthorized information disclosure and potential integrity compromise.

items.title: Crass: Non-ASCII characters cause superlinear CPU consumption
items.description:
### Impact

When parsing an input containing non-ASCII characters, inefficiencies in how Crass tracks the positions of multi-byte characters result in superlinear parsing time. An attacker-controlled input consisting of many non-ASCII characters could cause excessive CPU consumption and potentially denial of service.

### Patches

This is fixed in Crass 1.0.7.

### Workarounds

Avoid passing non-ASCII input to Crass. Or cultivate patience.

items.title: Crass: A large number of adjacent CSS comments can trigger a SystemStackError
items.description:
### Impact

When the `:preserve_comments` option is not enabled (which is the default behavior), Crass discards CSS comments by recursively consuming the next token. An attacker who provides a stylesheet containing a very large number of adjacent comments can cause excessive recursion and trigger a `SystemStackError`.

### Patches

This is fixed in Crass 1.0.7, which no longer recurses when discarding comments.

### Workarounds

Set the `:preserve_comments` option to `true` if this is acceptable to your use case (recursion doesn't occur when comments are preserved).

items.title: Crass: Deeply nested CSS blocks and functions can trigger a SystemStackError or excessive memory usage
items.description:
### Impact

Crass recursively parses CSS simple blocks and functions without a depth guard. An attacker-controlled value containing many deeply nested blocks can recurse until Ruby raises `SystemStackError: stack level too deep`, or can cause excessive memory usage.

### Patches

This is fixed in Crass 1.0.7, which adds a configurable depth limit with a conservative default.

### Workarounds

Add `SystemStackError` handling around Crass calls in your application. Buy more RAM.

items.description:
### Summary

Daptin's `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware) calls `golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage` on the raw `Accept-Language` header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. items.title: PocketMine-MP has potential memory/network vulnerability from repeated ResourcePackClientResponsePacket packets
items.description:
### Summary
During the resource pack stage of logging in, after the server sends `ResourcePackStackPacket`, a malicious client can send a batch of multiple `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket` packets with status `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket::STATUS_COMPLETED` causing the server to repeatedly execute pre-spawn progression.

###  Impact
Multiple `Player` objects can be created for just a single session, increasing memory usage and amplifying outbound network traffic from duplication of large pre-spawn packets such as `AvailableCommandsPacket` and `CreativeContentPacket`.

### Workarounds
Plugins can use their own `PacketHandler` classes that reject/ignore any extra `ResourcePackClientResponsePacket` packets.

### Patches
This issue was patched in https://github.com/pmmp/PocketMine-MP/commit/7a27894146a04964ab628ed9033140fdbf887ff3 and released in 5.44.2.

### Impact
In CMS 5, the password reset flow let a user with multi-factor authentication enabled change their password and get a logged-in session before completing multi-factor authentication. Exploiting this requires access to the user's email account. CMS 6 is not affected.
